name: mapscii
why: Renders the whole world map as braille characters in a terminal, a strange and beautiful transform of geography into text.

brief.what_it_is: MapSCII is a Node.js renderer that draws a world map inside a terminal. It takes OpenStreetMap-derived vector tiles, either from its bundled OSM2VectorTiles-based server or from any vector tile server you point it at, or from local VectorTile/MBTiles files. It converts the geometry into Braille characters, with plain ASCII and block-character modes also available, and displays it in xterm-compatible terminals. You navigate with arrow keys, the a/z zoom keys, or mouse drag and scroll. The README also says it can show points of interest around a location and that the styling can follow Mapbox Style specs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README gives no explicit motivation beyond its tagline, "The Whole World In Your Console", and its description as a vector tile to Braille and ASCII renderer for xterm-compatible terminals.
brief.how_it_works: The README names the pipeline through its libraries: vector-tile and pbf parse and decode Protobuf map tiles, and mbtiles reads MBTiles files. Earcut triangulates polygons, rbush provides spatial indexing for geometry and labels, and simplify-js and bresenham handle line simplification and point calculation. x256 maps colours to the nearest xterm-256 code, and term-mouse and keypress handle mouse and keyboard input. Downloaded tiles are cached in a location chosen by env-paths.

commands_seen.context: Connects to the public hosted MapSCII instance so you can try it without installing anything; the README says PuTTY is the option on Windows.
Runs MapSCII directly with a modern Node install, without a global install.
Installs MapSCII globally via npm; needs Node.js 10 or newer.
The README's fallback for macOS or permission errors during the global npm install.
Installs the snap package on supported Linux distros; the README says this snap is maintained by @nathanhaines.
Starts the interactive map in the terminal once installed.

brief.install_notes: Needs Node.js 10 or newer for the npm route. The snap route covers supported Linux distros. The README mentions possible sudo for permission errors on npm global installs. No API keys, accounts, or special hardware are mentioned. Custom tile servers, Mapbox styles, and offline MBTiles are optional configuration. Mouse control needs a terminal that supports mouse events.
brief.standout: It turns geography into Braille glyphs, so a whole map renders as text in an ordinary terminal, and it can be reached over telnet with no client-side install. It is also written in pure JavaScript and uses Mapbox-style vector tiles.
brief.status: Unknown from the README alone. There is a Travis CI badge and a maintained snap package, but the page shows no release date, last commit, or version. The README also lists open TODOs, such as GeoJSON support and threaded tile downloads, that are not yet done.
brief.caveats: Mouse hover over labels and polygons is still a TODO. The README says the renderer is not yet optimised for large areas (issue #6). Tile download and processing is on the same thread (issue #3). Single vector-tile handling is unimplemented. Map data is ODbL-licensed OpenStreetMap data, and the cartography is CC BY-SA 2.0, so attribution and share-alike conditions apply to the data. The README describes the terminal support as compatible with 'most Linux and OSX terminals', with no mention of Windows apart from using PuTTY for telnet. The sudo advice for npm is given without further explanation.

entry.title: mapscii
entry.tldr: Draws a pannable, zoomable world map in your terminal using Braille characters, and you can try it over telnet with nothing installed.
entry.deeper_look:
MapSCII is a Node.js renderer that takes OpenStreetMap-derived vector tiles and turns them into text. Each Braille character carries a 2x4 grid of dots, so a terminal cell becomes a small canvas for drawing coastlines, roads and borders. Plain ASCII and block-character modes are also available. It runs in xterm-compatible terminals and is steered with arrow keys, the a and z keys to zoom, or mouse drag and scroll.

The tiles can come from the bundled OSM2VectorTiles-based server, from any vector tile server you point it at, or from local VectorTile and MBTiles files. The README says styling can follow the Mapbox Style spec, and that it can show points of interest around a location.

The idea underneath is the pipeline from geography to glyphs. Protobuf tiles are decoded, polygons are triangulated, lines are simplified and rasterised with Bresenham, and the result is quantised to xterm-256 colours. Each step is a small, well-known algorithm from cartography or graphics. Reading the dependency list (vector-tile, earcut, rbush, simplify-js, bresenham) is a tidy tour of how a web map works, done without a browser.

The README gives no motivation beyond its tagline, "The Whole World In Your Console". It is also "100% pure JavaScript!"
entry.install:
brew install mapscii
# needs Node (installed as a brew dependency); no account or API key. Mouse control needs a terminal that supports mouse events.

try_this.what_happens: Connects to the public hosted instance, so you see the Braille world map without installing anything.
Starts the interactive map locally; pan with arrow keys, zoom with a and z, or drag and scroll with the mouse.
Runs it straight through npm without a global install.

entry.whats_unique: It turns a whole-world vector map into Braille glyphs in an ordinary terminal, and it is reachable over telnet with no client-side install.
entry.caveats: The README lists open TODOs: it is not yet optimised for large areas, tile downloading shares the main thread, and no release date or last commit is visible, so its maintenance status is unclear.
